\noindent Dear Editors,

\vspace{0.6em}
I am pleased to submit the enclosed manuscript, ``98 Per Cent of the
Procedure, 26 Per Cent of the Code: The Enacted Law and the Applied Law in
\nJudgments{} Judgments,'' for consideration in the \emph{Journal of Legal
Analysis}.

\vspace{0.5em}
Empirical work on legislation measures what states enact, and empirical work
on courts measures what judges decide. Joining the two requires both corpora
for one jurisdiction at article level, which is why it is rarely done. Saudi
Arabia now permits it: the state has codified much of its private and
commercial law within a decade, and its Ministry of Justice publishes
commercial judgments in full text. The article links \nCitations{} statutory
citations in \nJudgments{} published judgments to \nRegistryArticles{}
articles across \nInstruments{} instruments, and reports what the link shows.

\vspace{0.5em}
The central result compares two instruments to themselves, so it depends on
no choice of denominator. The Commercial Courts Law, which tells the court
how to proceed, has \nCCLShare{} per cent of its articles cited in the
corpus. The Civil Transactions Law --- the codification of Saudi private law,
and the instrument the commercial court's own jurisdiction clause names ---
has \nCivilShare{} per cent of its \nCivilArticles{}. Across the statute book
\nArticlesCitedShare{} per cent of articles are ever cited; within the
jurisdiction the statute draws for itself, \nScopeNarrowShare{} per cent. The obvious objection to the wider figures, that the published record
is commercial while the denominator is not, is answered by rebuilding the
denominator from the jurisdiction clause under two readings and by a fourth
denominator that concedes the objection outright.

\vspace{0.5em}
Two further results may interest referees. Segmenting each judgment at its
own headings shows the narrowing to happen at the bench rather than the bar:
the court's reasons are more procedural than the statement of the case, not
less, and \nRecitalOnlyInstruments{} instruments appear in the statement of
the case and never once in a court's reasoning. And amendment activity predicts neither citation nor
its absence: the pooled ratio suggesting otherwise is a composition effect
that disappears under a within-instrument control.

\vspace{0.5em}
The method section reports three defects that produced confident wrong
answers before they were found --- the direction of containment when matching
a citation to an instrument, anaphora resolved by recency rather than by
kind, and the segment before the reasons being the court's writing rather
than the parties' --- because each would change a reported result and none is
visible in a match rate. Three claims an earlier draft made were withdrawn
during checking.

\vspace{0.5em}
\textbf{Data and code.} The article is written to the data and code
availability policy the journal applies. Both corpora, the extraction and
matching code, and the scripts that generate every number in the manuscript
are public at
\url{https://github.com/Abdullah-m7/saudi-legal-corpus-ai}, with a
replication guide that reproduces each reported figure from the deposited
data. No number in the manuscript is typed by hand: all are generated into a
file of macros and typeset from it, and a check refuses to build a manuscript
that types one anyway.

\vspace{0.5em}
\textbf{Use of AI tools.} As the journal requires, I disclose that the
analysis code and drafts of the manuscript were produced with the assistance
of a large language model (Anthropic's Claude), working under my direction. I
designed the study, framed the questions, verified each result against the
corpus, and take responsibility for the content. The manuscript carries the
same disclosure. No measurement in the article is produced by a language
model; every figure is computed by the deposited code from the deposited
data.

\vspace{0.5em}
The manuscript is not under consideration elsewhere and has not been
published. I have no competing interests and received no funding for this
work. I am an independent researcher without institutional support, and if
the article is accepted I will apply to Oxford University Press for a waiver
of the open access charge.
